title: Debt Problems of the Richest Countries Are Trickling Down to the Poorest
summary: The debt load of developing countries jumped to $9.4 trillion as high interest rates and other global shocks batter their economies.

It’s hard to find a government these days that is not struggling with crushing public debt.


The financial problems of wealthier nations have been monopolizing the spotlight. The[United States](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/01/19/business/economy/trump-economy.html) ,[Britain](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/11/06/business/britain-economy-interest-rates.html) ,[France,](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/12/business/france-fitch-debt-rating.html) Italy,[China](https://carnegieendowment.org/china-financial-markets/2026/08/who-paid-for-chinas-last-debt-cleanup-and-who-will-pay-for-the-next) and[Japan](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/05/28/business/japan-debt.html) are all facing record or near-record debt levels. The fallout has been painfully visible in France, where anger at rising costs and crumbling public facilities and services helped provoke violent protests and a general strike in recent weeks.


But rich countries’ fiscal problems do not just pool at home; they trickle down to amplify the financial pressures on low and middle-income countries.


The result is that less-well off nations are borrowing more and paying more for their loans. Their combined debt surged last year to $9.4 trillion, according to a World Bank[report](https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2026/11/05/developing-countries-external-debt-surges-to-record-9-4-trillion) this month.


The poorest of the poor countries fare the worst: They are facing interest rates not seen since the late 1980s.


Many of the causes are beyond their control. A series of crises, beginning with the Covid-19 pandemic, and continuing with energy shocks, supply chain disruptions and rising prices stemming from the wars in Ukraine and Iran have strained national budgets and pumped up debts.
